title: The Will of the Fens
premise: When the coffin of Merrick Halloway, founder of the fen-town of Saltmere, is found empty during a centennial exhumation, hotel concierge Kestrel Villalobos is quietly hired by the town council to find out why—before the scandal destroys Saltmere's tourism-dependent future. Kestrel's investigation reveals that thirty years ago, a young woman named Ada Quill vanished, and several of the town's most respected elders wove an alibi together to hide what happened. As Kestrel closes in on the truth—that Halloway murdered Ada and his friends buried her body in his place and spirited his corpse away—they realize the conspiracy's last living member will kill again to keep it sealed. In the end, Kestrel must choose between delivering justice that will ruin the town that finally made them feel they belong, or protecting a lie; they choose truth, exposing the crime at cost of their own place in Saltmere, but finding belonging instead with Ada's surviving sister.
about_author: Ansel Eastwick is the pen name of a former night-desk clerk at a coastal inn who spent a decade listening to guests confess things they'd never tell anyone awake. They write mysteries set in small places where everyone knows your name and no one knows your business.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Third-person limited from Kestrel's POV. During Saltmere's centennial ceremony, the exhumed coffin of founder Merrick Halloway is opened before the whole town—and contains only river stones weighted with lead. Kestrel, working the reception desk at the Marsh King Hotel, watches every face in the crowd and notices three people leave without surprise. The beat: fascination sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: A Concierge's Ledger
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The panicked town council privately retains Kestrel—whose off-the-books reputation for solving guests' problems precedes them—to resolve the matter discreetly within two weeks. Kestrel reviews their mental ledger of the crowd: Mayor Odette Crane, gravedigger Silas Fenwick, and archivist Mrs. Tansy all reacted wrong. The beat: professional pride masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Kestrel canvasses the town under the pretext of centennial interviews. Everyone repeats the same polished story of Halloway's death: heart failure, closed casket per his wishes, quick burial. The uniformity itself becomes evidence—who coaches an entire town? An old barmaid lets slip one unscripted word: 'Ada.' The beat: unease beneath nostalgia.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Left
chapters.summary: Kestrel digs into records and finds Ada Quill, a nineteen-year-old hotel maid who disappeared in 1994, ruled a runaway. Her file is thin—too thin, with a page visibly razored out. Kestrel learns Ada had a sister, Wren, who still lives across the fens and never believed the runaway story. The beat: the thrill of a real thread.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: POV shifts briefly to Wren Quill, then back to Kestrel. Kestrel visits Wren's isolated cottage; Wren is hostile, having watched journalists come and go for decades. But when Kestrel mentions the empty coffin, Wren goes pale and says only: 'So he didn't stay buried either.' She agrees to talk—if Kestrel swears the truth comes out, whatever it costs. The beat: reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: Alibis Woven Tight
chapters.summary: Kestrel reconstructs the night Ada vanished: a harvest dance at the Marsh King, six witnesses whose accounts align with suspicious perfection. Cross-referencing old guest registers from the hotel's basement archive, Kestrel finds someone checked in that night under a false name—a signature Kestrel recognizes as Mrs. Tansy's handwriting. The beat: the past pressing close.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Confession
chapters.summary: Kestrel confronts Tansy gently; the elderly woman, relieved after thirty years, admits she falsified the register on Halloway's orders but claims she never knew why. She gives Kestrel a key to a storage room Halloway kept at the cannery, begging Kestrel not to make her testify. Two days later, Tansy dies in her sleep. The beat: guilt curdling into fear.

chapters.title: What the Cannery Kept
chapters.summary: Kestrel breaks into the derelict cannery and finds Halloway's storage room: Ada's belongings, a bloodstained dress hem, and Halloway's private journal hinting at 'the arrangement' with five signatories. Before Kestrel can photograph everything, someone sets fire to the building. Kestrel escapes with the journal but loses the physical evidence. The beat: terror and resolve.

chapters.title: Five Signatures
chapters.summary: The journal names initials, not names. Kestrel matches them: Halloway, Tansy (dead), Mayor Crane's father, the late police chief, and one living unknown—'D.F.' Suspicion falls on Silas Fenwick, the gravedigger, who dug Halloway's grave and now tends it like a shrine. Kestrel begins watching him. The beat: narrowing circles.

chapters.title: The Man Who Digs
chapters.summary: Silas's POV chapter. We learn Silas was seventeen in 1994, saw Halloway with Ada's body, and was coerced into silence—he has spent thirty years digging graves as penance. He knows someone is burning through the conspiracy's edges and decides to act first, mailing an anonymous letter to Mayor Crane warning that 'the concierge knows.' The beat: tragic complicity.

chapters.title: Pressure from Above
chapters.summary: Mayor Crane summons Kestrel, sweetly doubling the fee while making clear the town wants a tidy answer—runaway girl, opportunistic grave robbery, case closed. Kestrel realizes the council isn't seeking truth but containment, and that their employer may be the enemy. That night, Kestrel's hotel room is searched. The beat: betrayal of trust.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: Hotel owner Marisol, Kestrel's only friend in Saltmere, warns them to drop it—the Marsh King's survival depends on the town's image, and Marisol's own father signed the journal. She offers Kestrel a choice: stay quiet and keep the life they've built, or keep digging and lose everything. Kestrel, who has never belonged anywhere, feels the full weight of the offer. The beat: heartbreak.

chapters.title: The Second Death
chapters.summary: Silas Fenwick is found drowned in the fen, staged as an accident—but Kestrel notices his boots are dry-stored, meaning he walked in willingly or was carried. Among his effects: a photograph of Ada, and a note reading 'I kept my watch.' Someone is eliminating witnesses faster than Kestrel can interview them. The beat: grief and urgency.

chapters.title: Reading the Fens
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Wren search the fenland where Silas 'kept watch,' following his habitually worn path to a peat bank. Beneath disturbed ground, Wren recognizes a scrap of fabric—Ada's. The body isn't there; Silas moved it years ago to protect it from the conspirators. A fresh spade-cut shows someone else came looking recently. The beat: solemn discovery.

chapters.title: Unraveling D.F.
chapters.summary: Process-of-elimination chapter. Kestrel reexamines the journal's fifth initial and realizes the handwriting analysis points not to Fenwick but to the current police sergeant, Dane Ferris—son of the late chief, raised inside the lie, now protecting his father's legacy. Ferris has been one step ahead because he's been reading Kestrel's reports via the mayor. The beat: cold clarity.

chapters.title: Cornered
chapters.summary: Ferris detains Kestrel on manufactured charges of tampering with a heritage site, buying time to destroy remaining evidence. In holding, Kestrel passes a coded message through a hotel bellhop to Wren and Marisol. Marisol, choosing loyalty to Kestrel over her father's memory, retrieves the journal from its hiding place. The beat: fear transmuted into defiance.

chapters.title: What Silas Buried
chapters.summary: Wren leads police—real county investigators, bypassing Ferris—to the true grave site Silas relocated: Ada Quill's remains, preserved in peat, with injuries consistent with homicide. Forensics confirm death by violence in 1994. The runaway story collapses publicly. Ferris, exposed, burns the town archives and flees into the fens. The beat: grim vindication.

chapters.title: The Chase Through the Reeds
chapters.summary: Climax begins. Kestrel, knowing the fens better than Ferris from months of walking them, tracks him to the drowning pool where Silas died. Ferris, desperate, tries to force Kestrel into the mire; Kestrel uses a concierge's knowledge—every boardwalk plank, every soft patch—to turn the trap, and Ferris is arrested by arriving county officers as the tide rises. The beat: adrenaline and moral clarity.

chapters.title: The Mayor's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Confronted with the journal and forensics, Mayor Crane confesses her father's role and her own decades of cover-up, resigning publicly. The town reels: its founding myth is a murder story. Some thank Kestrel; more shun them. Marisol keeps the hotel but must let Kestrel go to survive the fallout. The beat: bitter triumph.

chapters.title: Ada's Funeral
chapters.summary: Ada Quill is finally buried, her name read aloud at a crowded service Kestrel attends from the back row. Wren speaks; the town listens. Kestrel, unemployed and unwelcome, prepares to leave Saltmere on the morning coach, feeling the familiar ache of exile—but also, for the first time, peace with the cost. The beat: mourning turned to honor.

chapters.title: An Open Door
chapters.summary: As Kestrel waits at the coach stop, Wren arrives with a proposition: help her establish a memorial and legal fund in Ada's name—work that needs someone who notices everything. Kestrel hesitates, then stays. Belonging, they realize, was never the town's to give; it's built with the few who share your truths. The beat: quiet hope.

chapters.title: The Will of the Fens
chapters.summary: Epilogue, spring. Kestrel runs a small inquiry office above Wren's cottage, taking cases no one else wants. A new guest checks into the Marsh King with a lie ready on their lips, and Kestrel, invited to consult, watches the town practice its imperfect, honest new way of remembering. The fens keep their dead now—named, mourned, witnessed. The beat: earned belonging.
